# Hepatic encephalopathy

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the liver > Hepatic encephalopathy*

[Original Article Link](/library/9G0NY3)

---

## Summary

Hepatic <u>encephalopathy</u> refers to <u>brain</u> dysfunction in the presence of underlying <u>liver</u> disease. It is common in patients with <u>cirrhosis</u>. Precipitating factors include infections, <u>gastrointestinal bleeding</u>, and <u>constipation</u>. Pathophysiology is complex and not completely understood, however, the accumulation of <u>ammonia</u> in the blood plays a central role. Clinical features vary and may include confusion, <u>asterixis</u>, and even <u>coma</u>. Diagnosis of <u>overt hepatic encephalopathy</u> is based on the presence of characteristic clinical features but the diagnosis of <u>covert hepatic encephalopathy</u> requires psychometric testing to confirm a diagnosis. Treatment consists of identifying and treating the underlying cause (e.g., <u>GI bleeding</u>) and pharmacotherapy with <u>disaccharide</u> <u>laxatives</u> (e.g., <u>lactulose</u>) and/or <u>rifaximin</u>. <u>Liver transplant</u> is the only curative therapy.

---

## Definitions

<u>Brain</u> dysfunction (e.g., fluctuations in mental status and cognitive function) in the presence of <u>liver</u> insufficiency (e.g., <u>cirrhosis</u>) [[2]](/library/1gY28o)[[3]](/library/mqbV_u)

---

## Etiology

* Caused by underlying <u>liver</u> dysfunction (e.g., <u>cirrhosis</u>, <u>acute liver failure</u>)

* Precipitating factors include: [[4]](/library/QsXuuz)

* Increased absorption or production of <u>ammonia</u>

* Infections (e.g., <u>spontaneous bacterial peritonitis</u>, <u>SIRS</u>)

* <u>Gastrointestinal bleeding</u>

* <u>Constipation</u>

* Increased dietary protein intake

* <u>Hypokalemia</u>

* Decreased metabolism and clearance of <u>ammonia</u>

* <u>Renal failure</u>

* <u>PVT</u>

* <u>Portosystemic shunts</u> (e.g., after <u>TIPS</u> placement)

* <u>Hypovolemia</u> (<u>dehydration</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>, vomit)

* <u>Metabolic alkalosis</u>

* <u>Diuretic</u> use (<u>hypokalemia</u>, <u>hyponatremia</u>)

---

## Pathophysiology

* <u>Cirrhosis</u> → ↓ hepatic metabolism and <u>portosystemic shunt</u> → accumulation of <u>neurotoxic</u> metabolites, including <u>ammonia</u> (<u>NH<sub>3</sub></u>) → <u>ammonia</u> crosses <u>blood-brain barrier</u>, is taken up by <u>astrocytes</u>, and converted to <u>glutamine</u> → ↑ <u>osmotic pressure</u> and cellular swelling → <u>cerebral edema</u> and ↑ <u>intracranial pressure</u> → neurological deterioration

* Metabolic effects:

* <u>Hypokalemia</u> → compensatory shift of <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> ions out of the cells and H<sup>+</sup> ions into the cells to maintain electroneutrality → intracellular <u>acidosis</u> → stimulates tubular cells to produce more <u>ammonia</u> → neurological deterioration

* <u>Metabolic alkalosis</u> → decreased H<sup>+</sup> ion availability → decreased conversion of <u>ammonia</u> (<u>NH<sub>3</sub></u>) to ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) → increased levels of <u>ammonia</u>, which diffuses freely across the <u>blood-brain barrier</u> → neurological deterioration

---

## Clinical features

Symptoms are usually reversible and may be nonspecific.




* Fatigue, <u>lethargy</u>, <u>apathy</u>

* Altered <u>levels of consciousness</u>, ranging from mild confusion to <u>stupor</u> or <u>coma</u>

* Disoriented

* Irritability

* <u>Memory</u> loss

* Impaired sleeping patterns

* Socially aberrant behavior (e.g., urinating/defecating in public, shouting at strangers)

* Slurred speech

* <u>Asterixis</u>

* Muscle rigidity

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[2]](/library/1gY28o)[[6]](/library/B9XzpZ0)




* <u>Diagnosis of hepatic encephalopathy</u> is largely clinical and based on ruling out alternate explanations for <u>altered mental status</u>.

* It is critical to identify the precipitating factor (e.g., <u>GI bleed</u>).

* The diagnosis of <u>covert hepatic encephalopathy</u> requires psychometric testing, which is usually carried out by a specialist. [[2]](/library/1gY28o)[[6]](/library/B9XzpZ0)





### Initial evaluation [[2]](/library/1gY28o)[[7]](/library/AoXRe_)




* <u>Physical examination</u>

* Assessment of mental status (e.g., orientation, <u>Glasgow coma scale</u>)

* Evaluation for <u>asterixis</u>

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* <u>CBC</u>, <u>BMP</u>: rule out <u>hypoglycemia</u>, <u>hyponatremia</u>, <u>uremia</u>, ketoacidosis, and <u>hypercalcemia</u>

* <u>CRP</u>, <u>WBC count</u>, <u>blood cultures</u>, <u>urinalysis</u>, and culture: evaluate for underlying infection

* Blood <u>alcohol</u>: rule out <u>alcohol intoxication</u>

* <u>Ammonia</u> level: low/normal level may be helpful to rule out hepatic <u>encephalopathy</u>  [[2]](/library/1gY28o)[[5]](/library/cq1ax30)





### Additional evaluation




* Imaging: 

* <u>Chest x-ray</u> to rule out infection

* Consider an abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> to assess for <u>ascites</u> and <u>PVT</u>

* Consider CT or <u>MRI</u> head to rule out alternate etiology. [[8]](/library/NBX-a00)

* Psychometric tests (e.g., <u>number connection test</u>): usually carried out by specialists to quantify the severity of hepatic <u>encephalopathy</u>





> [!TIP]
> Serum <u>ammonia</u> levels are usually elevated in hepatic <u>encephalopathy</u>. However, elevated levels are not diagnostic and the magnitude of elevation does not correlate with the degree of <u>encephalopathy</u>. [[7]](/library/AoXRe_)

---

## Treatment

### General measures [[2]](/library/1gY28o)[[9]](/library/hydcUs0)




* Avoid further insult (e.g., <u>hepatotoxic</u> medication, <u>alcohol</u>).

* Treat precipitating factors (e.g., <u>hypovolemia</u>, <u>constipation</u>, <u>GI bleeding</u>, <u>electrolyte</u> disturbances).  [[2]](/library/1gY28o)

* Nutritional recommendations [[9]](/library/hydcUs0)

* Routinely assess for <u>malnutrition</u>. See “<u>Clinical evaluation of malnutrition in adults</u>.”

* Dietary protein restriction is not recommended.

* Consider <u>branched-chain amino acid</u> supplementation if available.

* <u>Liver transplant</u> is the ultimate treatment.





> [!TIP]
> Identification and treatment of infection and/or bleeding is critical, as these precipitants are associated with high mortality. [[5]](/library/cq1ax30)




### Pharmacotherapy   [[2]](/library/1gY28o)




* Lactulose: a synthetic <u>disaccharide</u> <u>laxative</u>

* Indications: first-line for ; prevention and <u>treatment of hepatic encephalopathy</u>

* Routes: <u>lactulose</u> PO DOSAGE or <u>lactulose</u> PR DOSAGE  [[10]](/library/AkdRqJ0)

* Mechanism: <u>Lactulose</u> is converted to <u>lactic acid</u> by intestinal flora → acidification in the gut → conversion of <u>ammonia</u> (<u>NH<sub>3</sub></u>) to ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) → ammonium is excreted in the feces → decreased blood <u>ammonia</u> concentration → decreased absorption of <u>ammonia</u> in the bowel → improved <u>symptoms of hepatic encephalopathy</u>

* Rifaximin (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE ;  : a broad-spectrum, nonabsorbable oral <u>antibiotic</u> [[11]](/library/dxcove0)

* Reduces the number of <u>ammonia</u>-producing intestinal bacteria

* May be added to <u>lactulose</u> if a second episode occurs to prevent recurrent episodes of hepatic <u>encephalopathy</u> [[2]](/library/1gY28o)





> [!WARNING]
> Oral administration of medications may not be safe in patients with <u>overt hepatic encephalopathy</u> at risk of <u>aspiration</u>. Consider alternative administration routes.




### <u>Liver transplant</u> [[5]](/library/cq1ax30)




* Only definitive treatment option  [[5]](/library/cq1ax30)

* Consider in all patients with recurrent or persistent HE

* Referral for evaluation by transplant center is recommended for all patients with first episode of <u>overt hepatic encephalopathy</u>





### Disposition [[5]](/library/cq1ax30)




* Multiple factors play a role in disposition/triage (e.g., <u>GCS</u> level/ability to protect <u>airway</u>, severity of hepatic <u>encephalopathy</u>, prognosis, <u>medical futility</u>)

* <u>ICU</u> management is generally recommended in patients with <u>overt hepatic encephalopathy</u> who are at risk of <u>aspiration</u> [[5]](/library/cq1ax30)





### Prevention [[2]](/library/1gY28o)[[5]](/library/cq1ax30)




* After the initial episode of <u>overt hepatic encephalopathy</u>: <u>lactulose</u> DOSAGE

* For recurrent episodes: combination therapy of <u>lactulose</u> DOSAGE PLUS <u>rifaximin</u> DOSAGE

* Patients with <u>cirrhosis</u> presenting with <u>GI bleeding</u>: consider rapid removal of blood from <u>GI tract</u> via e.g., <u>lactulose</u> by <u>NG tube</u> or enema [[5]](/library/cq1ax30)
